title: Pluggable parse layer for multiformat logs with stable correlation mapping
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem: Production teams send a mix of JSON, plain-text, syslog, journald, and protobuf-encoded logs to our telemetry pipeline. Current ingest relies on brittle per-source heuristics resulting in lost correlation IDs, high parse-failure rates, and hotspots when CPU-intensive parsing runs inline on gateway nodes.

Goal: Implement a pluggable "parse layer" that can normalize multi-format logs into a canonical structured envelope, expose a stable canonical correlation_id for each event (canonicalization rules and rotation handling), and provide a safe extension model for customer parsers. The layer should be efficient (low per-event CPU), observable (parse success/failure metrics + sample traces), and compatible with existing downstream sinks (Loki/ELK/Kafka).
acceptance_criteria: Incoming events (JSON, key=value, syslog, journald, protobuf) are normalized into a canonical envelope with fields: timestamp, tenant_id, service, level, message, attributes, canonical_correlation_id
Canonical correlation ID produced for 99.9% of events for supported formats via deterministic mapping rules or fallback generation; mapping rules documented
Parse failure rate < 0.2% for known sources + operators can see failure samples in Console -> Logs Explorer
WASM-based custom parser interface implemented and validated with two sample parsers (nginx key=value and internal protobuf schema)
End-to-end tests that send mixed-format payloads through gateway -> parser -> loki sink, validating fields and correlation_id stability
Metrics emitted: parse_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), parse_failures_total, canonical_id_generation_total, custom_parser_execution_time_ms
Graceful degradation: when parsing CPU exceeds threshold, gateway returns structured minimal envelope and marks event as 'parsed_lite' and increments a backpressure metric
tasks: Design canonical envelope schema and deterministic canonical_id algorithm (Maya, 2 days)
Prototype Rust/WASM parser host with sandboxing and time/memory limits (Liam, 5 days)
Implement format detectors and fast-path JSON/native parser that avoids double-copying (R&D) (3 days)
Add metrics, logs, and sampling hooks for parse failures to Console dashboard (Observability UI) (2 days)
Integration tests against loki/elastic sinks and tenant routing (4 days)
Create runbook for high parse-failure incidents and mitigation steps (Oncall) (1 day)
Document parser extension API and publish two example parsers to docs repo (Documentation) (2 days)
notes: Trade-offs considered: doing heavy parsing at edge vs lightweight canonicalization + downstream enrichment. We favor lightweight canonicalization at gateway to preserve latency SLOs and offload expensive schema-heavy enrichment to a worker tier.

Performance approach: adopt a tiered parser chain: 1) cheap detector -> 2) zero-copy JSON fast-path -> 3) WASM parser for non-standard formats -> 4) fallback generator. This limits CPU tail latency and keeps p95 parse latency < 5ms for common payloads.

Correlation id strategy: canonicalize upstream ids by applying versioned normalization rules (strip prefixes, map uuid variants, normalize hex case, align timestamp-embedded ids). For rotated ids, keep last_seen window of 5 minutes to tie related events; for missing ids, generate deterministic UUID v5 from tenant+trace-hash to enable joinability while avoiding collision across tenants.

Safety: WASM host will enforce 20ms execution time, 16MB memory per invocation, and limit syscalls. Parsers signed by Redwood devs will be allowed elevated limits; customer-submitted parsers use strict sandbox.

Schema registry: propose adding a lightweight 'parse schema registry' (yaml-based) for internal teams to register expected top-level keys and example payloads. This helps lower parse-failure noise and accelerate onboarding.

Backpressure: if gateway CPU sustained > 70% for parse threads, switch to 'lite' mode that only extracts correlation_id (if present) and timestamp, tags event parsed_lite=true and routes to separate queue for later reprocessing.

Migration: we'll run parser in parallel for 2 weeks (dual-write) where both old and new envelopes are emitted to a kafka topic suffixed with '-v2' to validate downstream compatibility before cutting over.

Open question: should we persist canonical_id mapping state in a small LRU cache (local) to avoid repeated generation for high-cardinality ids? Prototype suggests small benefit but increases memory pressure; default is stateless deterministic generation plus optional local cache toggle per instance.
